shape.name: Receptive Skills — Reading
shape.description: A reading lesson built around a true story about Ebola, with a listening main task and a structured discussion finale.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Reading is taught through explicit question-type strategies before the task, then applied to a listening read-along of the same text. A differentiated B2 challenge text extends fast finishers. The lesson closes with an opinion-reason-evidence discussion on a topical vaccine question, so reading feeds directly into speaking.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end, students will [read + discuss with evidence].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Receptive Skills — Reading
Why should we be so scared of Ebola?

stages.stage: Lead-in: What do we know about Ebola?
stages.stage_aim: Activate prior knowledge and generate interest in the topic.
procedure: Show the splash slide (Ebola virus micrograph). Ask: "What do you see? What might this lesson be about?" Let students speculate freely.
Advance to the title slide: "Why should we be so scared of Ebola?" Confirm the theme.
Show the death image (safe-burial workers with a coffin). Open-class discussion: "What is Ebola? How deadly is it? What are the workers doing?" Accept all answers; do not correct yet.

stages.stage_aim: Pre-teach four words that block comprehension of the text.
procedure: Show the red transition "Let's check your word knowledge".
Present each word with the 3-click reveal: phonemic script, then the word, then a context sentence.
Words: outbreak, veterinarian, strain, decontamination. Context sentences are neutral everyday examples — they must not reveal the reading's story. Do NOT teach "raw" — it is tested in Question 5.

stages.stage_aim: Introduce the question types in the reading and how to answer them.
procedure: Detail questions (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q6): find the exact fact; scan for key words.
Main idea and purpose (Q4): ask what the passage shows overall.
Vocabulary in context (Q5): guess the meaning from the surrounding clues.
Inference and attitude (Q7, Q8): read between the lines; judge the writer's tone.
After each strategy, complete the "Try it" demo table on the slideshow.

stages.stage: Main task: listen, read and check
stages.stage_aim: Listen to the narrated text while following along, then self-check answers.
procedure: Play the monolog audio: the narrator (a Benedict Cumberbatch voice clone) reads the B1 text aloud.
Students follow along on the worksheet and complete or confirm their answers.
Gallery walk: students walk around and check their answers against the pre-printed answer posters on the walls.
Fast finishers: grab a B2 text from the back of the room and complete it with 10 minutes to go.

stages.stage_aim: Give a structured opinion using evidence from the text.
procedure: Show the O-R-E structure: Opinion, Reason, Evidence (yellow label under the opening question).
Drill the interaction language: I agree with you because... / I see your point, but... / So we both think...
Topic: "There is a lot of criticism about vaccines these days. Should we be suspicious of them?" Students give an opinion, a reason, and evidence.

metadata.topic: Why should we be so scared of Ebola?
materials: B1 reading: "The Scientist Who Caught Ebola on Her Glove" (adapted from The Hot Zone by Richard Preston, 1989 Reston outbreak) — article + 8 multiple-choice questions
B2 challenge reading (extension for fast finishers)
Slideshow: Why should we be so scared of Ebola? (28 slides)
Worksheet: B1 questions (and B2 challenge questions)
Pre-printed B1 answer posters for the gallery walk
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, students will be able to read and understand an article about the Ebola virus, identify common reading question types, and give a structured opinion using evidence from the text.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Students will practise listening while reading and use language of agreement and disagreement in discussion.
answer_key: 1. D — No one got very sick. The virus in Reston was a special strain, and it never made anyone seriously ill.
2. A — Any error might be fatal. Jaax worked with deadly monkey blood in a protective suit, and one small mistake could cost her life.
3. C — The writer gives details about her safety equipment. He lists the protective suit, thick rubber gloves, and mask to make the danger concrete.
4. D — The writer shows how a scientist almost became infected. The whole passage tells the near-miss: a hole in her glove and blood on an open cut.
5. C — "Raw" means new and painful, not protected by skin. The cut on her palm was still raw and unhealed.
6. B — She filled the glove with water to test its condition. If the water leaked out, the glove had a hole.
7. A — Jaax felt frightened and unsure. She could not tell if the blood under her glove was the monkey's or her own.
8. B — The tone is dramatic and admiring. The writer tells the near-disaster with suspense and respect for Jaax.
